si.short: The international system of units, adopted in 1960: kilogram, metre, second, mole and units built from them, such as the joule (J), watt (W) and newton (N).

vo2max.short: The highest rate at which the body can take up and use oxygen, in L·min⁻¹ (absolute) or mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (per kg of body mass).

joule.short: The SI unit of energy and work: the work done by a force of 1 newton over 1 metre. 1 kJ = 1,000 J; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

watt.short: The SI unit of power: one joule per second (W = J·s⁻¹). Power is how fast work is done.

gross-efficiency.short: Mechanical power ÷ metabolic power. In cycling about 20%: the rest of the energy becomes heat.

ftp.short: The power a cyclist should be able to hold for about an hour, usually taken as 95% of a 20-minute best. Many riders last well under an hour at it. Used to set training zones.

critical-power.short: The power where the power–duration curve (best power against how long it can be held) levels off. Below it an effort can settle into a steady state; above it fatigue keeps building and the effort has a time limit.

heart-rate-reserve.short: Maximum heart rate minus resting heart rate. A target at x% HRR is: resting HR + x% × HRR (the Karvonen method).

percentage-point.short: The plain difference between two percentages: 20% to 22% is +2 percentage points, which is a 10% relative rise.

half-life.short: For an exponential process, the time for the remaining gap to halve. t½ = 0.69 × τ.

log-scale.short: An axis where equal distances mean equal ratios (×10 or ×2), so seconds and hours fit on one graph.

o2-deficit.short: At the start of exercise, the oxygen that would have been used if VO2 had jumped straight to the demand: the area between demand and actual VO2. Fast energy sources that need no oxygen cover the gap.

confounder.short: A third factor linked to both the exposure and the outcome, which makes them look related when one may not cause the other (e.g. talent links training hours and VO2max).

metabolic-energy.short: The energy the body releases by breaking down its fuels (carbohydrate, fat) to do work and stay alive; per second it is metabolic power. Muscles turn only about a fifth of it into work; the rest becomes heat.

vo2.short: The rate at which the body takes up and uses oxygen, in L·min⁻¹ or mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. It rises with exercise intensity up to a ceiling, VO2max.

vo2-kinetics.short: How fast oxygen uptake rises to meet a new workload, usually given as a time constant (τ). Faster kinetics mean a smaller oxygen deficit at the start of exercise.

buffer.short: A substance that soaks up acid and so stops body fluids becoming too acidic. Bicarbonate in the blood is the main one; when it soaks up acid it releases extra CO₂, which is breathed out.

correlation.short: How closely two measures move together, from −1 to +1: r near 0 means no straight-line link, near ±1 a tight one. A correlation alone doesn't show that one causes the other.
